why_it_matters: It is the clearest delivery skill found: platform checks on the output file, numbers in the report, and a contact sheet the agent must view after any picture change.
fit_notes: Needs FFmpeg 6.1+ and Python 3.10+ locally; no cloud. It tells the agent to use only its scripts and never raw ffmpeg, so a job the 42 tools do not cover stops there. A good last step after any renderer: hand it the MP4 and ask for a platform check. I did not run it.

claims.text: Before reporting done, the agent checks the output against a named platform.
claims.quote: 5. **Check** with `check.py OUTPUT --platform X --expect-identity S:M`

claims.text: After any picture change it must view a tiled contact sheet, and say so when it could not look.
claims.quote: 8. **Look** after any picture change: `look.py OUTPUT --tiles 3x2`, view the PNG, name it in `Look:`;

claims.text: It burns caption words as written and never shortens them to fit.
claims.quote: - **The words in a caption** — burned as written; never rewrite or shorten them, even to "make it fit".
claims.locator: skills/ffmpeg-skill/SKILL.md, section on what the agent never changes

checked.what: skills/ffmpeg-skill/SKILL.md and README.md against the three claims

title: motion-design skill (LottieFiles)
summary: A tool-agnostic motion design skill: director notes, easing and timing tables, patterns, and a quality checklist with severity tiers.
why_it_matters: Its checklist turns motion taste into checks an agent can tick before rendering, with a stated severity for each miss.
fit_notes: Written for UI motion first: some checks (prefers-reduced-motion, pausable animations over 5 s) do not apply to a rendered MP4; skip them. The checklist is for the agent to read code or frames against; the skill ships no tool that measures a render. Its ban on linear easing matches tool:haidrrrry/claude-remotion-skill.

claims.text: Its checklist caps the total stagger of a sequence below 500 ms and marks more as critical.
claims.quote: - [ ] Stagger total <500ms

claims.text: It allows at most a third of the elements on screen to move at the same time.
claims.quote: - [ ] 1/3 rule (density): max 1/3 elements active simultaneously

checked.what: quality-checklist.md and README.md against both claims

title: Manim Community Edition
summary: A Python animation engine for explanatory math video, forked from 3b1b/manim in 2020 and run by a community team. The `manim` CLI renders a Scene class to a video file.
why_it_matters: The usual route for diagram and equation animation written by an agent in Python, with a one-flag way to get the last frame as a PNG.
fit_notes: `manim -s` (or `--format=png`) writes only the last frame, and `-ql` renders at low quality; both cut the review loop for an agent. Install needs system packages (the README points to per-OS docs; LaTeX only for TeX). The README says a major refactor is in progress, so APIs may move. Do not mix its install steps with 3b1b/manim: the package names differ and both READMEs warn of breakage.

related.note: Fork of it; different package and CLI.

claims.quote: It was forked from 3b1b/manim, a tool originally created and open-sourced by Grant Sanderson

claims.text: The CLI can skip the animation and save only the final frame as a PNG.
claims.quote: -s, --save_last_frame          Fast-forward animations and save the last frame
claims.locator: docs.manim.community, Configuration guide, command line help

claims.text: Using the other project's install instructions breaks the install.

title: Revideo
summary: A TypeScript engine for video in code, forked from Motion Canvas, with a headless renderVideo() API and a React player for preview. It renders through Node and a headless browser.
why_it_matters: It gives the Motion Canvas authoring model a render call an agent can run, and it names Claude and Codex as authors.
fit_notes: The repo moved from redotvideo/revideo to midrender/revideo and is the engine behind the Midrender product. It counts renders through PostHog unless you set DISABLE_TELEMETRY=true. The README says it borrows from Remotion and Rive while its docs say it is a Motion Canvas fork; both can be true, but expect Motion Canvas APIs. I did not find a documented single-frame still command in what I read.

title: editly
summary: A Node.js tool that builds a video from a JSON5 edit spec of clips, images, titles, audio and GL transitions, streaming through ffmpeg.
why_it_matters: A declarative format an agent can write without a frame model, with a `--fast` flag for a low-cost preview render.
fit_notes: Needs ffmpeg and ffprobe on PATH and a native headless-gl build; the README's troubleshooting is mostly native-module errors. Without `--fast`, every clip is converted to the first input's size and frame rate, which surprises mixed inputs. The last push to the repo was 2025-05-12 (GitHub API, read 2026-11-12), so I marked it dormant. It is a single-maintainer project by its README.

title: Motion Canvas
summary: A TypeScript library that programs vector animation with generators, plus a browser editor with live preview. Rendering is started from the editor.
why_it_matters: Good for code explainers synced to voice-over, but its render step is a button in a browser editor, which an agent cannot press without browser automation.
fit_notes: For an agent that must produce the MP4 itself, use Revideo, its fork with a headless render API. The default exporter writes an image sequence; MP4 needs the FFmpeg exporter. Snapshots of the current frame go to /still in the output folder, again from the editor. I did not check for a documented headless or CLI render path beyond the rendering page.

title: Remotion
summary: A React framework for video. Each frame is a component rendered from the frame number; the CLI renders the frames in headless Chrome and encodes MP4.
why_it_matters: The most established code renderer an agent can drive locally, and the one most skills target. Its licence is the first thing to check before company work.
fit_notes: Free for a person or a company of up to 3 employees; a bigger company needs a paid Company License, and the FAQ adds a per-render plan for automations (code that calls renderMedia() and similar). The repo says a changed licence ships with Remotion 5.0 (PR #3750); re-read LICENSE.md when you upgrade. For agent feedback, `npx remotion still <entry> <id> out.png --frame=N` gives one PNG without a full render, and `npx remotion render <id> out/frames --frames=0,30,90 --image-format=png` gives several (v4.0.502+). Animations written with CSS keyframes or setTimeout flicker or freeze because tabs render frames out of order.

related.note: Kinetograph states it renders Remotion projects without a browser.

claims.text: The free licence covers individuals, for-profit companies with up to 3 employees, non-profits and evaluation; others need a Company License.
claims.quote: a for-profit organization with up to 3 employees

claims.text: A single frame can be rendered to an image from the CLI, which gives an agent a frame to inspect before the full render.
claims.quote: Render a still frame based on the entry point, the composition ID and save it to the output location.

claims.text: CSS animations and timers are not captured correctly because frames render independently and out of order.
claims.quote: Remotion renders each frame independently. Frame 30 might be rendered before frame 10, or frame 50 might be rendered twice.

checked.what: LICENSE.md, license/faq.mdx, cli/still.mdx and troubleshooting/css-animations.mdx against the claims

title: MoviePy
summary: A Python library for cutting, compositing and titling video. It loads frames as numpy arrays and encodes the result through ffmpeg.
why_it_matters: Easy for an agent to script in Python, but agent training data is full of v1 code that v2 broke.
fit_notes: Tell the agent to target MoviePy v2 and to read the v1-to-v2 guide: its README example uses v2 names such as `subclipped` and `with_volume_scaled`, and code written against v1 docs fails. It is slower than ffmpeg alone, so use it for logic and let ffmpeg do heavy filters. TextClip takes a font file path, so ship the .ttf with the project. The README asks for maintainers. I did not check a still-frame API.

claims.text: Version 2.0 introduced major breaking changes and v1 is no longer maintained.
claims.quote: MoviePy recently upgraded to v2.0, introducing major breaking changes.

claims.text: Its own README says it is slower than using ffmpeg directly.
claims.quote: albeit slower than using ffmpeg directly due to heavier data import/export operations
